listen_text: Definition of reduct and expansion. Suppose language L is contained in language L prime, structure M is an L structure, and structure M prime is an L prime structure. Structure M is the reduct of M prime to L, and M prime is an expansion of M to L prime, if and only if four conditions hold in order. First, their domains are equal. Second, every constant c of L has the same interpretation in M and M prime. Third, every function f of L has the same interpretation in both structures. Fourth, every predicate P of L has the same interpretation in both structures.
long_description: A smaller-language structure is the reduct of a larger-language structure precisely when their domains and all shared symbol interpretations agree.
name: defn

listen_text: Proposition. If the L structure M is a reduct of the L prime structure M prime, then for every sentence A of L, M satisfies A if and only if M prime satisfies A.
long_description: A structure and its expansion satisfy exactly the same sentences from the smaller language.
name: prop

listen_text: Unsolved exercise. Prove the preceding proposition that a reduct and its expansion satisfy the same sentences of the smaller language.
long_description: Unsolved exercise asking for a proof that reducts preserve all sentences of the smaller language.
name: prob

listen_text: Definition. Let M be an L structure. Let L prime be L expanded by one new n place predicate P, and let R be an n place relation on the domain of M. The expansion of M by R denotes the L prime structure M prime whose interpretation of P is R.
long_description: Defines the notation for expanding a structure by interpreting one newly added predicate as a chosen relation.
name: defn

listen_text: Definition of substructure. Let M and M prime be structures for the same language L. Structure M is a substructure of M prime, and M prime is an extension of M, if and only if four conditions hold. First, the domain of M is contained in the domain of M prime. Second, each constant of L has the same interpretation in both structures. Third, for every n place function and every n tuple from the domain of M, the function values in M and M prime are equal. Fourth, for every n place predicate and every n tuple from the domain of M, that tuple belongs to the predicate interpretation in M if and only if it belongs to the predicate interpretation in M prime.
long_description: A substructure has a smaller domain, agrees on constants, restricts functions, and agrees on predicates over its domain.
name: defn

listen_text: Theorem. If a set Gamma of sentences has arbitrarily large finite models, then Gamma has an infinite model.
long_description: Arbitrarily large finite models imply the existence of an infinite model.
name: thm

listen_text: Proposition. In no first-order language is there a sentence A that is true in a structure M if and only if the domain of M is infinite.
long_description: No single first-order sentence is true exactly in structures with infinite domain.
name: prop

listen_text: Definition of elementary equivalence. Given structures M and M prime for the same language L, M is elementarily equivalent to M prime if and only if, for every sentence A of L, M satisfies A exactly when M prime satisfies A.
long_description: Two structures in the same language are elementarily equivalent when they agree on every sentence.
name: defn

listen_text: Definition of isomorphism. Structures M and M prime for the same language L are isomorphic if and only if there is a function h from the domain of M to the domain of M prime satisfying five conditions. First, h is injective: if h of x equals h of y, then x equals y. Second, h is surjective: every y in the domain of M prime equals h of some x in the domain of M. Third, for every constant c, h applied to the interpretation of c in M equals its interpretation in M prime. Fourth, for every n place predicate P, a tuple a sub one through a sub n belongs to P in M if and only if the tuple of their h images belongs to P in M prime. Fifth, for every n place function f, applying h after f in M equals applying f in M prime to the h images of the arguments.
long_description: An isomorphism is a bijection of domains preserving constants, predicates, and functions.
name: defn

listen_text: Theorem. If structure M is isomorphic to structure M prime, then M is elementarily equivalent to M prime.
long_description: Isomorphism preserves every first-order sentence.
name: thm

accessible_name: Function-term values before and after an isomorphism
listen_text: Two aligned term-value equations. First, the value of the compound term t in M at assignment s is the interpretation of f in M applied to the values of component terms t sub one through t sub n in M at s. Second, the frozen source prints the value of t in M prime at h composed with s as the interpretation of f in M applied to the corresponding component values in M prime. That printed M is wrong because the left side is evaluated in M prime. The disclosed reader correction uses the interpretation of f in M prime and retains the frozen source equation separately.
long_description: Two aligned equations compare a compound term in M and M prime, with a disclosed wrong-structure correction in the second row.
name: align*

accessible_name: Inductive equality chain for compound term values
listen_text: Four-line equality chain. The frozen first line says h applied to the value of t in M at s equals h applied to the interpretation of f in M at the component values, but it omits the closing parenthesis for the outer h. The disclosed reader correction supplies that close and retains the source form. The second line uses preservation of the function interpretation to move h inside and apply f in M prime to the h images. The third line uses the induction hypothesis to replace those images by the values of t sub one through t sub n in M prime at h composed with s. The fourth line identifies the result as the value of t in M prime at h composed with s.
long_description: A four-line equality chain proves that an isomorphism carries compound-term values to their values in the target structure, with a disclosed parenthesis correction.
name: align

listen_text: Unsolved exercise. Carry out part b of the preceding isomorphism theorem in detail, and state where each of the five defining properties of an isomorphism is used.
long_description: Unsolved exercise asking for the formula case of isomorphism invariance and an accounting of all five isomorphism conditions.
name: prob

listen_text: Definition. An automorphism of a structure M is an isomorphism from M onto itself.
long_description: An automorphism is an isomorphism from a structure onto itself.
name: defn

listen_text: Unsolved exercise. Let X be a definable subset of a structure M, and let h be an automorphism of M. Show that X equals the set of h of x for x in X; equivalently, X is fixed under h.
long_description: Unsolved exercise asking to prove that every definable subset is fixed setwise by every automorphism.
name: prob

accessible_name: Definition of the theory of a structure
listen_text: Definition. Given a structure M, the theory of M is the set of sentences true in M. In set notation, it is the set of all sentences A such that M satisfies A.
long_description: The theory of M is the set of all sentences true in M.
name: defn

accessible_name: The theory of a structure is complete
listen_text: Proposition. For every structure M, the theory of M is complete.
long_description: Every structure decides each sentence, so its theory is complete.
name: prop

accessible_name: Models of a complete structural theory are elementarily equivalent
listen_text: Proposition. If structure N satisfies every sentence A that belongs to the theory of M, then M is elementarily equivalent to N.
long_description: Any structure satisfying every sentence true in M is elementarily equivalent to M.
name: prop

listen_text: Definition of partial isomorphism. Given structures M and N, a partial isomorphism from M to N is a finite partial function p from the domain of M into the domain of N satisfying the isomorphism conditions on its domain. First, p is injective. Second, for every constant c, whenever p is defined at the interpretation of c in M, its value is the interpretation of c in N. Third, for every n place predicate P and arguments a sub one through a sub n in the domain of p, their tuple belongs to P in M if and only if the tuple of their p images belongs to P in N. Fourth, for every n place function f and such arguments, p of the f value in M equals the f value in N of their p images. Finiteness means that the domain of p is finite.
long_description: A finite partial function is a partial isomorphism when it satisfies injectivity and the defined constant, predicate, and function preservation clauses.
name: defn

accessible_name: Definition of partial isomorphism between structures
listen_text: Definition. Structures M and N are partially isomorphic if and only if there is a nonempty set I of partial isomorphisms between them satisfying two back-and-forth clauses. Forth: for every p in I and every a in the domain of M, some q in I extends p and has a in its domain. Back: for every p in I and every b in the domain of N, some q in I extends p and has b in its range.
long_description: Two structures are partially isomorphic when a nonempty family of partial isomorphisms has the forth and back extension properties.
name: defn

accessible_name: Enumerable partially isomorphic structures are isomorphic
listen_text: Theorem. If structures M and N are partially isomorphic and both are enumerable, then M and N are isomorphic.
long_description: For enumerable structures, a back-and-forth family can be assembled into a total isomorphism.
name: thm

accessible_name: Exercise checking the back-and-forth union map
listen_text: Unsolved exercise. Prove in detail that the map p constructed in the theorem about enumerable partially isomorphic structures is an isomorphism.
long_description: Unsolved exercise asking to verify that the map constructed in the preceding theorem is an isomorphism.
name: prob

accessible_name: Partial isomorphism implies elementary equivalence in relational languages
listen_text: Theorem. Let M and N be structures for a purely relational language, meaning a language with predicates but no functions or constants. If M and N are partially isomorphic, then they are elementarily equivalent.
long_description: For purely relational languages, partially isomorphic structures agree on every first-order sentence.
name: thm

listen_text: Definition. The quantifier rank of a formula A is the greatest number of nested quantifiers in A, defined recursively, and is a natural number. Structures M and N are n equivalent if they agree on every sentence whose quantifier rank is at most n.
long_description: Quantifier rank measures nesting depth, and n equivalent structures agree on every sentence up to that rank.
name: defn

listen_text: Proposition. Let L be a finite purely relational language with finitely many predicates and constants and no functions. For every natural number n, up to logical equivalence there are only finitely many first-order sentences of L with quantifier rank at most n.
long_description: A finite relational language has only finitely many sentences of any fixed maximum quantifier rank, up to logical equivalence.
name: prop

accessible_name: Finite sequences over a structure domain
listen_text: Definition. For a structure M, the domain of M to the less-than-omega power is the set of all finite sequences of elements of its domain. Bold a, bold b, bold c, and so on range over such sequences. If sequence a is finite over M and a is in the domain of M, then sequence a followed by a denotes their concatenation.
long_description: Defines notation for finite sequences and for appending one element to a sequence.
name: defn

accessible_name: Recursive back-and-forth relations on finite sequences
listen_text: Definition. For structures M and N, define relations I sub n between equal-length finite sequences from their domains by recursion on n. Base clause: I sub zero holds of sequences a and b exactly when they satisfy the same atomic formulas in M and N; explicitly, if assignments s sub one and s sub two send each x sub i to a sub i and b sub i, then M satisfies an atomic formula A at s sub one if and only if N satisfies A at s sub two. Successor clause: I sub n plus one holds of a and b exactly when every element a of M has a matching element b of N for which I sub n holds of the two extended sequences, and conversely every element of N has a matching element of M.
long_description: Defines relations I sub n first by atomic agreement and then by mutual one-element extensions.
name: defn

accessible_name: Definition of back-and-forth equivalence at level n
listen_text: Definition. Write M is back-and-forth equivalent at level n to N when relation I sub n holds of the empty sequence and the empty sequence for M and N.
long_description: M and N are approximately equivalent at level n when I sub n relates their empty sequences.
name: defn

listen_text: Theorem. Let L be purely relational. If I sub n holds of sequences a and b, then for every formula A of quantifier rank at most n, M satisfies A at a if and only if N satisfies A at b. Here a satisfies A when any assignment sending each x sub i to a sub i satisfies A. If L is finite, the converse implication also holds.
long_description: I sub n implies agreement on formulas of rank at most n, with a converse for finite languages.
name: thm

accessible_name: Finite back-and-forth equivalence matches bounded elementary equivalence
listen_text: Corollary. If M and N are purely relational structures in a finite language, then M is back-and-forth equivalent at level n to N if and only if M and N are elementarily equivalent through quantifier rank n. In particular, M and N are elementarily equivalent if and only if they are back-and-forth equivalent at every level n.
long_description: In finite relational languages, level-n back-and-forth equivalence is exactly agreement through quantifier rank n.
name: cor

accessible_name: Definition of dense linear ordering without endpoints
listen_text: Definition. A dense linear ordering without endpoints is a structure with one binary relation, less than, satisfying six sentences. First, every x is not less than itself. Second, for all x, y, and z, if x is less than y and y is less than z, then x is less than z. Third, for all x and y, exactly one ordering comparison or equality places them: x is less than y, x equals y, or y is less than x. Fourth, every x has some greater y. Fifth, every x has some smaller y. Sixth, whenever x is less than y, there is a z strictly between x and y.
long_description: Six first-order axioms specify irreflexivity, transitivity, totality, no endpoints, and density.
name: defn

accessible_name: Cantor isomorphism theorem for countable dense orders
listen_text: Theorem. Any two enumerable dense linear orderings without endpoints are isomorphic.
long_description: Any two enumerable dense linear orders without endpoints are isomorphic.
name: thm

accessible_name: Exercise verifying the back property for dense orders
listen_text: Unsolved exercise. Complete the proof that any two enumerable dense linear orders without endpoints are isomorphic by verifying that the family I of partial isomorphisms satisfies the Back property.
long_description: Unsolved exercise asking to finish the Cantor back-and-forth proof by establishing the Back clause.
name: prob
